notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • The Peninsular Plateau is one of the oldest and most stable landmasses of India.
  • It is composed mainly of ancient crystalline, igneous and metamorphic rocks.
  • It formed part of the ancient Gondwana landmass.
  • It lies mainly south of the Northern Plains.
  • It has a broadly triangular shape.
  • The plateau is generally higher in the west and slopes gently toward the east.
  • Many major peninsular rivers therefore flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Peninsular Plateau → Ancient + Stable + Crystalline

2. Geological Age
  • The Peninsular Plateau is much older than the Himalayas.
  • It represents part of the ancient Indian shield.
  • Large parts have remained tectonically stable for a very long geological period.
  • Long erosion has reduced many former mountains into rounded hills and residual uplands.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Peninsular Plateau → Old

Himalayas → Young

3. Gondwana Connection
  • Peninsular India was part of Gondwana.
  • Gondwana also included parts of present-day Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica.
  • The Indian Plate later separated and moved northward.
4. General Shape
  • The plateau has a roughly triangular outline.
  • The broad base lies toward northern-central India.
  • It narrows southward toward the Indian Ocean.
5. General Elevation
  • Average elevation generally ranges from around 600 to 900 metres in many plateau regions.
  • Elevation varies widely.
  • Higher western margins are formed by the Western Ghats.
  • Plateau surfaces descend gradually eastward.
6. General Slope
  • Much of the Peninsular Plateau slopes from west to east.
  • Therefore, major rivers such as Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi flow eastward.
  • Narmada and Tapi are major west-flowing exceptions.
📌 Must-Memorise

General Slope → West to East

7. Major Divisions of Peninsular Plateau

The plateau is broadly divided into:

  • Central Highlands.
  • Deccan Plateau.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Central Highlands → North of Narmada

Deccan Plateau → South of Narmada

8. Narmada as a Major Divider
  • The Narmada valley forms an important physiographic dividing line.
  • Central Highlands lie mainly north of it.
  • Deccan Plateau lies mainly south of it.
  • Narmada flows westward through a rift valley.
9. Central Highlands
  • The Central Highlands occupy the northern part of the Peninsular Plateau.
  • They lie mainly north of the Narmada.
  • They include several plateaus and ranges.
  • Their general slope is toward the north and northeast in many sectors.
10. Major Components of Central Highlands

Important components include:

  • Malwa Plateau.
  • Bundelkhand Plateau.
  • Baghelkhand Plateau.
  • Chotanagpur Plateau.
  • Aravalli Range and associated uplands.
11. Malwa Plateau
  • Malwa Plateau lies mainly in western Madhya Pradesh and southeastern Rajasthan.
  • It is formed largely by volcanic basalt in many parts.
  • It lies north of the Vindhyan region.
  • Chambal and its tributaries drain much of the plateau.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Malwa Plateau → Madhya Pradesh + Rajasthan

12. Malwa Plateau Drainage

Important rivers include:

  • Chambal.
  • Kali Sindh.
  • Parbati.
  • Betwa in adjoining regions.
  • Many rivers ultimately join the Yamuna system.
13. Chambal River
  • Chambal is an important tributary of the Yamuna.
  • It drains parts of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.
  • The Chambal basin is famous for ravines and badland topography.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chambal → Ravines

14. Ravines
  • Ravines are deep narrow gullies formed by severe erosion.
  • They are especially developed along the Chambal region.
  • Repeated gully erosion creates badland terrain.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chambal Valley → Ravines / Badlands

15. Bundelkhand Plateau
  • Bundelkhand lies mainly in parts of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.
  • It consists of old crystalline rocks.
  • The terrain is rocky and dissected.
  • Water scarcity is a major problem in many areas.
16. Baghelkhand Plateau
  • Baghelkhand lies east of Bundelkhand.
  • It extends across parts of Madhya Pradesh and adjoining Uttar Pradesh.
  • It forms a transition toward the Chotanagpur region.
17. Chotanagpur Plateau
  • Chotanagpur Plateau lies mainly in Jharkhand.
  • It extends into adjoining Odisha, West Bengal and Chhattisgarh.
  • It is one of India's most mineral-rich regions.
  • It contains coal, iron ore, mica, bauxite and other mineral resources.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chotanagpur Plateau → Mineral Heartland

18. Chotanagpur Plateau Subdivisions

Important subdivisions include:

  • Ranchi Plateau.
  • Hazaribagh Plateau.
  • Kodarma region.
  • Singhbhum Plateau.
19. Damodar Valley
  • Damodar River flows through the Chotanagpur region.
  • The valley contains major coalfields.
  • It became an important centre of heavy industry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Damodar Valley → Coal + Industry

20. Important Coalfields of Chotanagpur Region

Major coalfields include:

  • Jharia.
  • Bokaro.
  • Giridih.
  • Raniganj in the adjoining eastern region.

Detailed mineral distribution will be covered later.

21. Aravalli Range
  • Aravalli is one of the oldest fold-mountain systems in India.
  • It runs broadly from Gujarat through Rajasthan toward Delhi.
  • It is highly eroded.
  • It forms an important western boundary of the Central Highlands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aravalli → Very Old Fold Mountain

22. Aravalli Orientation
  • Aravalli extends roughly southwest to northeast.
  • It influences drainage and desert margins in northwestern India.
23. Highest Peak of Aravalli
  • Guru Shikhar is the highest peak of the Aravalli Range.
  • It is located near Mount Abu in Rajasthan.
  • Its elevation is about 1,722 metres.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aravalli Highest Peak → Guru Shikhar

24. Mount Abu
  • Mount Abu is a hill station in Rajasthan.
  • It lies in the Aravalli Range.
  • Guru Shikhar is located nearby.
25. Vindhya Range
  • Vindhya lies north of the Narmada valley.
  • It extends across central India.
  • It forms part of the northern edge of the Peninsular Plateau.
  • It is lower and more dissected than major young mountain systems.
26. Satpura Range
  • Satpura lies south of the Narmada valley.
  • It extends broadly east-west across central India.
  • It forms a major highland between Narmada and Tapi valleys in several sections.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Narmada → Between Vindhya and Satpura

27. Maikal Range
  • Maikal Range lies in eastern Madhya Pradesh and adjoining Chhattisgarh.
  • It forms the eastern continuation of the Satpura system.
  • Amarkantak Plateau is associated with this region.
28. Amarkantak Plateau
  • Amarkantak lies in Madhya Pradesh.
  • It is an important watershed.
  • Narmada originates near Amarkantak.
  • Son also originates in the broader Amarkantak region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amarkantak → Narmada + Son Source Region

29. Deccan Plateau
  • Deccan Plateau occupies the major southern part of the Peninsular Plateau.
  • It lies mainly south of the Narmada.
  • It has a roughly triangular form.
  • Western Ghats bound it on the west.
  • Eastern Ghats form a discontinuous eastern margin.
30. Meaning of Deccan
  • The word Deccan derives from Dakshina, meaning south.
  • It broadly refers to the southern plateau region of India.
31. Deccan Trap
  • Deccan Plateau is not one single flat surface.
  • It contains numerous plateaus, ranges, valleys and lava-covered uplands.
32. Deccan Trap Region
  • Large parts of Maharashtra and adjoining states are covered by basaltic lava flows.
  • These lava flows are called the Deccan Traps.
  • They were formed by massive volcanic eruptions near the end of the Cretaceous period.
  • Repeated lava layers created step-like topography.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deccan Trap → Basaltic Lava

33. Meaning of Trap
  • The word trap comes from a term meaning stairs or steps.
  • Weathering of successive lava layers creates step-like landforms.
34. Black Soil Link
  • Weathering of basalt in the Deccan Trap region contributes to formation of black soil.
  • Black soil is highly important for cotton cultivation.
  • Detailed soil facts will be covered later.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Deccan Basalt → Black Soil → Cotton

35. Maharashtra Plateau
  • Maharashtra occupies a large part of the northwestern Deccan Plateau.
  • It consists extensively of basaltic Deccan Trap rocks.
  • Numerous east-flowing rivers originate near the Western Ghats.
36. Karnataka Plateau
  • Karnataka Plateau forms an important part of the southern Deccan.
  • It is divided broadly into:
  • Malnad.
  • Maidan.
37. Malnad
  • Malnad is the hilly western part of Karnataka.
  • It lies closer to the Western Ghats.
  • It receives relatively high rainfall.
  • Forests and plantation crops are important.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Malnad → Hilly + Wet

38. Maidan
  • Maidan is the relatively open plateau region east of Malnad.
  • It is lower and drier.
  • Agriculture is more extensive.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Malnad → West, hilly

Maidan → East, plateau plain

39. Telangana Plateau
  • Telangana Plateau is part of the northeastern Deccan.
  • It is underlain largely by ancient rocks.
  • Godavari and Krishna tributaries drain the region.
40. Andhra Plateau Uplands
  • Interior Andhra Pradesh contains plateau and upland extensions east of Karnataka and Telangana.
  • These areas gradually descend toward the Eastern Ghats and coastal plain.
41. Tamil Nadu Plateau
  • Interior Tamil Nadu contains uplands and plateau surfaces.
  • Much of western and northwestern Tamil Nadu is influenced by the Western and Eastern Ghats.
  • The plateau generally descends toward the eastern coastal plain.
📌 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Interior Tamil Nadu → Peninsular Plateau Extension

42. Western Ghats
  • Western Ghats form the western edge of the Deccan Plateau.
  • They run approximately parallel to the western coast.
  • They are also called Sahyadris in much of Maharashtra and Karnataka.
  • They are higher and more continuous than the Eastern Ghats.
📌 Must-Memorise

Western Ghats = Sahyadris

43. Length of Western Ghats
  • Western Ghats extend for approximately 1,600 km.
  • They run from the Tapi valley region southward to the Nilgiris and beyond through the southern highlands.
44. Western Ghats — Major Characteristics
  • Steep western slopes.
  • Gentler eastern slopes.
  • Strong orographic rainfall.
  • High biodiversity.
  • Numerous short west-flowing streams.
  • Sources of several major east-flowing rivers.
45. Western Ghats as Watershed

Many important rivers originate in or near the Western Ghats, including:

  • Godavari.
  • Krishna.
  • Kaveri.
  • Several west-flowing coastal rivers.
46. Important Western Ghats Sections

From north to south, important highland sections include:

  • Sahyadri.
  • Nilgiri Hills.
  • Anaimalai Hills.
  • Palani Hills.
  • Cardamom Hills.
47. Northern Western Ghats
  • Northern Western Ghats extend through Maharashtra and northern Karnataka.
  • They include basaltic escarpments and numerous passes.
  • The region is locally known as Sahyadri.
48. Important Western Ghats Passes

Important passes/gaps include:

  • Thal Ghat.
  • Bhor Ghat.
  • Palghat Gap.
  • Shencottah Gap.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Pass ↔ State/Route matching

49. Thal Ghat
  • Thal Ghat lies in Maharashtra.
  • It provides an important route between the Mumbai region and the interior Deccan.
50. Bhor Ghat
  • Bhor Ghat also lies in Maharashtra.
  • It historically provided an important transport route between Mumbai and Pune.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhor Ghat → Mumbai–Pune Route

51. Nilgiri Hills
  • Nilgiri Hills lie at the junction of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka.
  • They form the meeting zone of Western and Eastern Ghats.
  • They are an important highland region of southern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Western + Eastern Ghats → Nilgiris

52. Doddabetta
  • Doddabetta is the highest peak of the Nilgiri Hills.
  • It lies near Ooty in Tamil Nadu.
  • Its elevation is about 2,637 metres.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Nilgiri Highest Peak → Doddabetta → 2,637 m

53. Ooty
  • Udhagamandalam, commonly called Ooty, lies in the Nilgiri Hills.
  • It is one of Tamil Nadu's major hill stations.
  • It is located at high elevation in the Western Ghats system.
54. Palghat Gap
  • Palghat Gap is a major break in the Western Ghats.
  • It lies between the Nilgiri Hills and Anaimalai Hills.
  • It connects Kerala with Tamil Nadu.
  • It is important for transport.
  • It also allows movement of winds between the two sides of the Ghats.
📌 Must-Memorise

Palghat Gap → Nilgiri + Anaimalai

55. Palghat Gap Width
  • Palghat Gap is much broader than many other passes through the Western Ghats.
  • This makes it a major natural corridor between the west coast and Tamil Nadu interior.
56. Anaimalai Hills
  • Anaimalai Hills lie south of the Palghat Gap.
  • They extend across parts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
  • They contain some of the highest peaks of southern India.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anaimalai → South of Palghat Gap

57. Anamudi
  • Anamudi is the highest peak of the Western Ghats.
  • It is also the highest peak in peninsular India.
  • It lies in Kerala.
  • Its elevation is about 2,695 metres.
📌 Must-Memorise

Peninsular India's Highest Peak → Anamudi → 2,695 m

58. Anamudi Location Trap
  • Anamudi is not in Tamil Nadu.
  • It lies in Kerala.
  • Doddabetta is an important high peak in Tamil Nadu's Nilgiris.
59. Palani Hills
  • Palani Hills lie mainly in Tamil Nadu.
  • They form part of the southern Western Ghats.
  • Kodaikanal is located in the Palani Hills.
📌 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Kodaikanal → Palani Hills

60. Cardamom Hills
  • Cardamom Hills lie mainly in Kerala and adjoining Tamil Nadu highlands.
  • They form part of the southern Western Ghats.
  • Plantation agriculture is important in the region.
61. Shencottah Gap
  • Shencottah or Shenkottai Gap lies in the southern Western Ghats.
  • It connects southern Tamil Nadu with Kerala.
  • It is an important transport corridor.
📌 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Shenkottai Gap → Tamil Nadu–Kerala

62. Eastern Ghats
  • Eastern Ghats form a discontinuous chain of hills along eastern Peninsular India.
  • They are lower than Western Ghats.
  • Major rivers have cut through them.
  • They extend through parts of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eastern Ghats → Discontinuous

63. Why Eastern Ghats Are Discontinuous

Major rivers such as:

  • Mahanadi.
  • Godavari.
  • Krishna.
  • Kaveri.

cut through the Eastern Ghats on their way to the Bay of Bengal.

64. Eastern Ghats in Odisha

Important hill regions include:

  • Mahendragiri.
  • Koraput uplands.
  • Niyamgiri region.
65. Mahendragiri
  • Mahendragiri is an important peak in the Eastern Ghats of Odisha.
  • It is frequently asked in map-based geography.
66. Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh

Important ranges include:

  • Nallamala Hills.
  • Palkonda Range.
  • Velikonda Range.
  • Seshachalam Hills.
67. Nallamala Hills
  • Nallamala Hills lie mainly in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana region.
  • They form part of the Eastern Ghats.
  • Krishna River cuts through this broader hill system.
68. Seshachalam Hills
  • Seshachalam Hills lie in Andhra Pradesh.
  • Tirupati hills are associated with this range.
  • The region is part of the Eastern Ghats.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tirupati → Seshachalam Hills

69. Eastern Ghats in Tamil Nadu

Important hill groups include:

  • Javadi Hills.
  • Shevaroy Hills.
  • Kalrayan Hills.
  • Kolli Hills.
  • Pachamalai Hills.
  • Sirumalai in the broader eastern uplands.
70. Javadi Hills
  • Javadi Hills lie in northern Tamil Nadu.
  • They form part of the Eastern Ghats system.
71. Shevaroy Hills
  • Shevaroy Hills lie near Salem in Tamil Nadu.
  • Yercaud is located in the Shevaroy Hills.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Yercaud → Shevaroy Hills

72. Kolli Hills
  • Kolli Hills lie mainly in Namakkal district region of Tamil Nadu.
  • They form part of the Eastern Ghats.
73. Kalrayan Hills
  • Kalrayan Hills lie in northern-central Tamil Nadu.
  • They form part of the Eastern Ghats.
74. Pachamalai Hills
  • Pachamalai Hills lie in central Tamil Nadu.
  • They are part of the Eastern Ghats.
75. Western vs Eastern Ghats

Western Ghats:

  • Higher.
  • More continuous.
  • Steeper western slope.
  • Strong orographic barrier.
  • Greater average rainfall on western slopes.

Eastern Ghats:

  • Lower.
  • Discontinuous.
  • Cut by rivers.
  • Less effective as a continuous climatic barrier.
76. Highest Peak of Western Ghats
  • Anamudi → about 2,695 m.
  • Located in Kerala.
77. Important Tamil Nadu Peaks
  • Doddabetta → Nilgiris.
  • Mukurthi → Nilgiri region.
  • Velliangiri and other highlands occur along the Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu.
78. Deccan Plateau Rivers

Major east-flowing rivers include:

  • Godavari.
  • Krishna.
  • Kaveri.
  • Mahanadi from the broader peninsular uplands.

Major west-flowing rivers include:

  • Narmada.
  • Tapi.
79. Narmada Rift Valley
  • Narmada flows through a structural rift valley.
  • It runs between Vindhya and Satpura ranges.
  • It flows westward into the Arabian Sea.
📌 Must-Memorise

Narmada → Rift Valley → Westward

80. Tapi Rift Valley
  • Tapi also flows westward through a structurally controlled valley.
  • It lies south of the Satpura region.
  • It drains into the Arabian Sea.
81. Rift Valley
  • A rift valley is a long narrow depression formed by faulting and crustal movement.
  • Narmada and Tapi valleys are classic Indian examples.
82. Escarpment
  • An escarpment is a steep slope separating two relatively level surfaces.
  • The western edge of the Deccan Plateau forms a strong escarpment along the Western Ghats.
83. Residual Hills
  • Residual hills remain after prolonged erosion removes surrounding material.
  • Many ancient peninsular hill systems have been heavily denuded.
84. Inselberg
  • An inselberg is an isolated residual hill rising abruptly from a plain.
  • Such features occur in old erosional landscapes.
85. Peninsular Drainage Characteristics
  • Rivers generally have well-defined valleys.
  • Their courses are older and more mature than many Himalayan rivers.
  • They have relatively fixed channels.
  • Most depend heavily on monsoon rainfall.
86. Peninsular vs Himalayan Rivers

Peninsular rivers:

  • Older.
  • More fixed courses.
  • Mostly rain-fed.
  • Broad shallow valleys.
  • Lower erosion rates in many mature sections.

Himalayan rivers:

  • Perennial.
  • Glacier and snow-fed as well as rain-fed.
  • Deep gorges in mountains.
  • Large sediment loads.
87. Waterfalls of Peninsular Plateau
  • Uneven relief and resistant rock layers create waterfalls.
  • Major waterfalls are often associated with plateau edges and river breaks in slope.

Examples include:

  • Jog Falls.
  • Shivanasamudra Falls.
  • Hundru Falls.
  • Chitrakote Falls.
88. Jog Falls
  • Jog Falls is located on the Sharavathi River in Karnataka.
  • It lies in the Western Ghats region.
  • It is one of India's famous waterfalls.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jog Falls → Sharavathi → Karnataka

89. Shivanasamudra Falls
  • Shivanasamudra Falls is on the Kaveri River in Karnataka.
  • It is historically associated with early hydroelectric development.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shivanasamudra → Kaveri

90. Hundru Falls
  • Hundru Falls is located on the Subarnarekha River in Jharkhand.
  • It lies in the Chotanagpur Plateau.
91. Chitrakote Falls
  • Chitrakote Falls lies on the Indravati River in Chhattisgarh.
  • It is associated with the Bastar Plateau region.
92. Bastar Plateau
  • Bastar Plateau lies mainly in southern Chhattisgarh.
  • It is part of the broader peninsular uplands.
  • The region is forested and mineral-rich.
93. Meghalaya Plateau
  • Meghalaya Plateau is geographically an extension of the Peninsular Plateau.
  • It is separated from the Chotanagpur Plateau by the Garo-Rajmahal gap.
  • It includes:
  • Garo Hills.
  • Khasi Hills.
  • Jaintia Hills.
📌 Must-Memorise

Meghalaya Plateau → Extension of Peninsular Plateau

94. Garo-Khasi-Jaintia Hills

From west to east:

  • Garo.
  • Khasi.
  • Jaintia.
📌 TNPSC Memory

G → K → J

95. Khasi Hills
  • Khasi Hills lie in central Meghalaya.
  • Cherrapunji and Mawsynram are located in the Khasi Hills region.
  • The southern escarpment receives extremely heavy rainfall.
96. Mawsynram
  • Mawsynram lies in Meghalaya.
  • It is famous for exceptionally high average annual rainfall.
  • Its location on the southern Khasi Hills enhances orographic rainfall.
97. Rajmahal Hills
  • Rajmahal Hills lie in Jharkhand.
  • They are associated with basaltic volcanic rocks.
  • They occur near the Ganga valley.
98. Garo-Rajmahal Gap
  • The Meghalaya Plateau is separated from the main Peninsular Plateau by a low-lying gap.
  • This gap was later filled with alluvium in parts.
99. Mineral Wealth of Peninsular Plateau

The plateau contains major deposits of:

  • Iron ore.
  • Coal.
  • Manganese.
  • Bauxite.
  • Mica.
  • Copper.
  • Limestone.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Peninsular Plateau → India's Major Mineral Storehouse

100. Why Minerals Are Abundant
  • Ancient igneous and metamorphic rocks contain many metallic minerals.
  • Gondwana sedimentary basins contain major coal deposits.
  • Long geological history created diverse mineral formations.
101. Iron Ore Regions

Important plateau iron-ore areas occur in:

  • Odisha.
  • Jharkhand.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Karnataka.

Detailed distribution will be covered later.

102. Coal Regions

Important coal regions include:

  • Damodar Valley.
  • Son Valley.
  • Mahanadi basin.
  • Godavari valley.
103. Plateau and Industry

Mineral availability encouraged development of industries in regions such as:

  • Jamshedpur.
  • Bokaro.
  • Rourkela.
  • Bhilai.
  • Durgapur and adjoining industrial belt.
104. Plateau and Hydroelectricity
  • Steep river gradients provide hydropower potential.
  • Waterfalls and escarpments provide suitable sites.
  • Western Ghats and southern uplands have several hydroelectric projects.
105. Plateau and Agriculture

Important crops include:

  • Cotton.
  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Sugarcane in irrigated areas.
  • Coffee and spices in highland plantation regions.
106. Cotton and Plateau
  • Black soil of basaltic Deccan regions is particularly suitable for cotton.
  • Maharashtra, Gujarat and parts of Madhya Pradesh are major cotton regions.
107. Plantation Crops in Western Ghats

Important crops include:

  • Coffee.
  • Tea in suitable highlands.
  • Rubber in wetter southern areas.
  • Cardamom.
  • Pepper.
108. Coffee
  • Karnataka is India's major coffee-producing state.
  • Coffee grows especially well in shaded hill slopes of the Western Ghats.
109. Plateau and Forests
  • Western Ghats contain evergreen and moist deciduous forests.
  • Interior plateau regions include dry deciduous and thorn forests.
  • Eastern plateau regions retain large forested tracts.
110. Western Ghats Biodiversity
  • Western Ghats are globally recognised for high biodiversity and endemism.
  • They form part of the Western Ghats–Sri Lanka biodiversity hotspot.
  • Tamil Nadu includes important portions of this hotspot.
111. Nilgiri Biosphere Link
  • Nilgiri region spans parts of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka.
  • It is one of India's most important mountain-biodiversity landscapes.
112. Plateau Rainfall Pattern
  • Western slopes receive heavy southwest monsoon rainfall.
  • Interior Deccan lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats.
  • Rainfall generally decreases eastward immediately behind the Western Ghats before varying again farther east.
113. Rain Shadow
  • A rain-shadow region lies on the leeward side of a mountain.
  • Descending air becomes warmer and drier.
  • Parts of interior Karnataka and Tamil Nadu lie in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats.
📌 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Western Tamil Nadu Interior → Rain-Shadow Influence

114. Western Ghats and Monsoon
  • Moist southwest monsoon winds from the Arabian Sea strike the Western Ghats.
  • Air rises, cools and condenses.
  • Heavy rainfall occurs on windward slopes.
115. Plateau Soils

Major soil types include:

  • Black soil.
  • Red soil.
  • Laterite soil.
  • Parts of alluvial and mixed soils.

Detailed soil classification will be covered separately.

116. Red Soil
  • Red soils are widespread over ancient crystalline rocks.
  • Their red colour is mainly due to iron oxides.
  • They are common in parts of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and other plateau areas.
117. Laterite Soil
  • Laterite develops under conditions of high temperature and heavy rainfall with intense leaching.
  • It occurs in parts of the Western Ghats and other high-rainfall plateau areas.
118. Plateau Population Pattern
  • Population density is generally lower than in the Northern Plains.
  • River valleys, industrial centres and fertile basins have higher concentrations.
  • Rugged and forested areas are more sparsely populated.
119. Tribal Population
  • Several plateau and forest regions contain large tribal populations.
  • Chotanagpur, Bastar and central Indian uplands are particularly important.
  • Social-geography details will be covered later.
120. Transport Challenges
  • Uneven terrain makes transport more difficult than in the Northern Plains.
  • Ghats require passes, tunnels and steep gradients.
  • Natural gaps such as Palghat have major transport importance.
121. Transport Advantage of Gaps
  • Gaps provide lower-elevation routes through mountain barriers.
  • Railways and highways often follow these natural corridors.
122. Peninsular Plateau and Seismicity
  • The Peninsular Plateau is generally more stable than the Himalayas.
  • However, intraplate earthquakes do occur.
  • Stability does not mean zero seismic risk.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Peninsular India ≠ Earthquake-Free

123. Latur Earthquake Link
  • The 1993 Latur earthquake in Maharashtra demonstrated that damaging earthquakes can occur within Peninsular India.
  • It occurred away from active plate boundaries.
124. Koyna Seismicity
  • Koyna region in Maharashtra is known for significant seismic activity.
  • The 1967 Koyna earthquake is an important example associated with the Peninsular region.
125. Plateau Erosion

Long-term erosion has produced:

  • Rounded hills.
  • Broad valleys.
  • Residual uplands.
  • Ravines.
  • Waterfalls.
  • Dissected plateaus.
126. Dissected Plateau
  • A dissected plateau is deeply cut by rivers and erosion.
  • Chotanagpur Plateau is a classic Indian example.
127. Plateau vs Plain

Plateau:

  • Elevated.
  • Uneven.
  • Old hard rocks.
  • Minerals abundant.

Plain:

  • Low relief.
  • Flat.
  • Mostly depositional in northern India.
  • Agriculture and transport easier.
128. Plateau vs Himalayas

Peninsular Plateau:

  • Ancient.
  • Stable.
  • Eroded.
  • Lower relief.

Himalayas:

  • Young.
  • Tectonically active.
  • Folded.
  • Very high relief.

135. Tamil Nadu Plateau Geography

Important TNPSC facts:

  • Nilgiris form a major western highland.
  • Doddabetta is the highest Nilgiri peak.
  • Anaimalai Hills lie south of Palghat Gap.
  • Palani Hills contain Kodaikanal.
  • Shevaroy Hills contain Yercaud.
  • Javadi, Kalrayan, Kolli and Pachamalai belong to the Eastern Ghats system.
  • Palghat and Shenkottai are important gaps.
  • Tamil Nadu's interior lies largely in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats during the southwest monsoon.
